extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and astronomers studying lunar theory / celestial mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Derive and compute the Moon's distance, variation (equation of the center), node motion, and inclination-variation using Newtonian geometric mechanics (areal law, curvature relations, perturbing solar force decomposition) with elliptic approximations and numerical evaluation. Applies the geometric constructions and series approximations presented in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areal law for lunar motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Area, quam Luna radio ad Terram ducto, singulis temporis momentis, describit, est ut motus horarius Lunæ & quadratum distantiæ Lunæ à Terrâ conjunctim
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use areal description with the radius drawn to the Earth: the instantaneous area swept in a time is proportional jointly to the Moon's hourly motion and the square of its distance from Earth. This is the fundamental relation used throughout to relate local angular motion, areal momentum, and distance when deriving distances and variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent lunar diameter inversely proportional to distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc datur Lunæ diameter apparens: quippe quæ sit reciprocè ut ipsius distantia à Terra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent angular diameter varies inversely with Earth–Moon distance; use this to relate observational angular sizes to computed distances (used for checking the derived distance ratios such as syzygies vs quadratures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature proportionality (attraction / velocity^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curvatura Trajectoriæ, quam mobile, si secundum Trajectoriæ illius perpendiculum trahatur, describit, est ut attractio directè & quadratum velocitatis inversè.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To relate local curvature of the Moon's path to forces and speed: curvature ∝ attraction / v^2. Use this to compare curvatures at different configurations (syzygies vs quadratures) given differing attractive forces and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature via limiting sines/tangents of contact angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Curvaturas linearum pono esse inter se in ultima proportione Sinuum vel Tangentium angulorum contactuum ad radios æquales, ubi radii illi in infinitum diminuuntur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute curvatures by taking the limit of ratios of sines or tangents of contact angles as reference radii shrink to zero; use contact-angle sine/tangent relations (and similar small-angle approximations) to pass from chord/tangent geometry to curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume elliptic orbit when true figure unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoniam figura orbis Lunaris ignoratur, hujus vice assumamus Ellipsin DBCA, in cujus centro S Terra collocetur, & cujus axis major DC Quadraturis, minor AB Syzygiis interjaceat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the true lunar orbit figure is unknown, assume an ellipse centered at S (Earth) with major/minor axes aligned to quadratures/syzygies respectively; then deduce ratios and curvatures under that ellipse assumption and compare with observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Sun–Moon lines as parallel to Earth–Sun line (small-inclination approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: in hoc calculo & eo omni qui sequitur, considero lineas omnes à Luna ad Solem ductas tanquam parallelas lineæ quæ à Terra ad Solem ducitur, propterea quod inclinatio tantum ferè minuit effectus omnes in aliquibus casibus, quantum auget in aliis; & Nodorum motus mediocres quærimus, neglectis istiusmodi minutiis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For simplifying perturbation calculations, treat Moon→Sun lines as parallel to Earth→Sun line (i.e., neglect small inclination-induced differences). This approximation omits minute corrections that would otherwise complicate algebra but are negligible for the mean nodal motions sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute lunar distance ratio (syzygies vs quadratures) from areal and velocity relations
rubrics_metrics.description: distantia Lunæ à Terrâ est in ratione compositâ ex dimidiatâ ratione Areæ directè & dimidiatâ ratione motus horarii inversè ... Est igitur distantia Lunæ à Terra in Syzygiis ad ipsius distantiam in Quadraturis ... vel numeris rotundis ut 69 ad 70.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine areal law and observed (or derived) hourly motion ratios in syzygies vs quadratures to compute the ratio of lunar distances; numerical outcome here is approximately 69:70 (syzygy : quadrature). Use the compositional proportion given (half power on area direct, half power on hourly motion inverse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of lunar variation: ellipse shape and areal-momentum inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Oritur hæc inæqualitas partim ex forma Elliptica orbis Lunaris, partim ex inæqualitate momentorum areæ, quam Luna radio ad Terram ducto describit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two separate contributors to the Moon's equation (variation/inequality): (1) orbital ellipticity and (2) non-uniform areal momentum (areal speed variations). Quantify each and combine (e.g., derive tangent corrections) to get numerical variation (here ≈ 35'9").

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust tangents to account for areal momentum excess (numerical tangent correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debet autem descriptio areæ CSP, in progressu Lunæ à Quadratura ad Syzygiam, ea ratione accelerari, ut ejus momentum in Syzygia Lunæ sit ad ejus momentum in Quadratura ut 11073 ad 10973 ... id quod satis accuratè fiet, si tangens anguli CSP diminuatur in dimidiata ratione numeri 10973 ad numerum 11073...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To model the areal-momentum acceleration between quadrature and syzygy, reduce the tangent of the relevant angle by the indicated ratio (10973/11073 half-wise) to account for increased areal momentum near syzygy and compute the resulting angular variation (example yields variation ≈32'31" then adjusted to ≈35'9" after accounting for Earth's motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Node-motion arises from two solar perturbing components; mean node velocity proportional to product of geometric sines
rubrics_metrics.description: Et vis Solis ad perturbandum motum Lunæ ... duplex erit, altera lineæ 2IT vel 2Kp, altera lineæ PI proportionalis. ... Est igitur velocitas Nodorum ut IT × PH & Sinus anguli STN conjunctim, sive ut contentum sub sinubus trium angulorum TPI, PTN & STN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the solar perturbing force into two components; the nodal precession (instantaneous node velocity) is proportional to the transverse perturbation factor IT, the perpendicular lever PH, and the sine of the inclination-related angle STN — equivalently to the product of sines of the three indicated angles. Use the specified geometric construction to evaluate these factors for numerical node-rate estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for node motion sign reversal when angle sign changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Et quoties signum anguli alicujus de affirmativo in negativum, deque negativo in affirmativum mutatur, debebit motus regressivus in progressivum & progressivus in regressivum mutari.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one of the governing angles changes sign, the sense of nodal motion inverts (regressive ↔ progressive). Apply this rule in determining whether nodes appear to advance or regress depending on lunar configuration relative to nodes and quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean hourly node motion in a given node position equals one-half the hourly motion at lunar syzygies (circular approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In data quavis Nodorum positione, motus horarius mediocris est semissis motus horarii in Syzygiis Lunæ, ideoque est ad 16". 35"′. 16 iv . 36 v . ut quadratum Sinus distantiæ Nodorum à Syzygiis ad quadratum Radii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the simplifying circular-orbit assumption and neglecting minute terms, the mean hourly nodal motion at any node position equals half the hourly motion that would be measured when the Moon is at syzygy; use this relation as a baseline before applying elliptic corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic correction to node motion scales by axis ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: motus mediocris Nodorum in Ellipsi erit ad motum mediocrem Nodorum in circulo, ut Ellipsis ad circulum, id est ut Ta ad TA, seu 68 11/12 ad 69 11/12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When switching from circular to elliptic lunar orbit, scale mean node motions by the ratio of ellipse to circumscribed circle (i.e., axis ratio). Numerically, the correction here reduces node motion slightly (factor ≈ 68 11/12 / 69 11/12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute mean annual node motion by summing areal contributions (sector-area method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus medius annuus est summa motuum omnium horariorum mediocrium in anno ... Et summa omnium horariorum motuum mediocrium ab initio, ut summa omnium arearum aYZA, id est ut area NAZ ... Motus autem horarius, rectangulo maximo respondens, erat 16". 16"′. 36 iv . 48 v . Et hic motus, anno toto sidereo ... fit 39 gr. 38′. 5". 39"′.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute annual mean node motion by integrating (summing) the hourly mean motions over the year using associated sector areas; use ratio of sector-area sum to total circle area to get the annual motion. The text provides steps and numerical evaluation leading to a sidereal annual node motion near 19°18'0".22"'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of series (infinite series) to compute small area corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Jam verò si circuli radius AT ponatur 1, erit area semicirculi 1,570796; & area figuræ NeFnT, per methodum Serierum infinitarum quæsita, prodibit 0,1188478.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small-area (noncircular) corrections in the nodal equation, compute the required area via infinite-series expansion (power series) and evaluate numerically. The text demonstrates this to obtain the correction area used in the annual node-motion computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric construction for true nodal equation (annual) via circle and tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: Centro C, intervallo quovis CD, describatur circulus BEFD. Producatur DC ad A, ut sit AB ad AC ut motus medius ad semissem motus veri mediocris ... dein per punctum D ducatur infinita Gg, quæ tangat circulum in D ... & agatur AE vel AF secans perpendiculum DG in G; & capiatur angulus qui sit ad motum Nodi inter ipsius Syzygias (id est ad 9 gr. 10′. 40".) ut tangens DG ad circuli BED circumferentiam totam, atque angulus iste ad motum medium Nodi addatur; habebitur eorum motus verus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct area-based computation is cumbersome, perform the proposed Euclidean geometric construction (circle, tangent, chosen proportional segments) to obtain the true (corrected) annual nodal motion. This is an algorithmic geometric procedure for translating mean to true nodal motion incorporating the computed equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monthly nodal equation negligible for lunar-latitude determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Est & æquatio menstrua, sed quæ ad inventionem Latitudinis Lunæ minimè necessaria est. Nam cum Variatio inclinationis Orbis Lunaris ad planum Eclipticæ duplici inæqualitati obnoxia sit, alteri annuæ, alteri autem menstruæ; hujus menstrua inæqualitas & æquatio menstrua Nodorum ita se mutuò contemperant & corrigunt, ut ambæ in determinanda Latitudine Lunæ negligi possint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a monthly equation of node motion exists, it may be neglected when determining lunar latitude because its effect largely cancels with the monthly inequality of inclination; use only the annual equation for latitude computations unless extreme precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hourly variation of inclination computed from perturbation geometry (proportional formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hæc ita se habent ex Hypothesi quod Luna in Orbe circulari uniformiter gyratur ... erit angulus GPg (seu inclinationis horaria Variatio) ad angulum 33". 10"′. 33 iv . ut IT × AZ × TG × Pp ÷ PG ad AT cub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the instantaneous hourly change of orbital inclination via the specified proportional formula involving geometric perturbation factors (IT, AZ, TG, Pp, PG) scaled to the reference angle 33"10'33 iv. Use this local variation and integrate/sum to get total variation over the node passage; the text carries through to a total variation ≈164" (2'44").

rubrics_metrics.name: Total inclination variation between quadrature and syzygy obtained by summing hourly variations
rubrics_metrics.description: summa omnium Variationum horariarum, quo tempore Luna in hoc situ Nodorum transit à Quadratura ad Syzygiam, (id est spatio horarum 177 1/6,) erit ad summam totidem angulorum 33". 10"′. 33 iv . seu 5878"½, ut summa omnium sinuum duplicatæ distantiæ Lunæ à Quadraturis ducta in Pp ÷ PG ad summam totidem diametrorum; ... Variatio tota, ex summa omnium horariarum Variationum tempore prædicto conflata, est 164" , seu 2′. 44".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate (sum) the instantaneous hourly inclination-variations across the lunar transit from quadrature to syzygy (approx. 177 1/6 hours) using the sine-of-duplicated-distance weighting to obtain the total inclination change. The worked example yields ≈164" (2'44"), and further adjustments for node position produce the maximal variation values quoted later (e.g., ~16'24").

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction to find inclination at a given time via trigonometric/geometric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit AD Sinus inclinationis maximæ, & AB Sinus Inclinationis minimæ. Bisecetur BD in C, & centro C, intervallo BC, describatur Circulus BGD. In AC capiatur CE in ea ratione ad EB quam EB habet ad 2 BA: Et si dato tempore constituatur angulus AEG æqualis duplicatæ distantiæ Nodorum à Quadraturis, & ad AD demittatur perpendiculum GH: erit AH Sinus inclinationis quæsitæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute the instantaneous inclination at a given time, perform this explicit geometric construction: choose CE in AC with specified proportion, construct angle AEG equal to twice the nodal distance from quadrature, drop perpendicular GH to AD and read AH as the sine of the desired inclination. The proposition gives the algebraic justification and shows how to handle changes in nodal distance uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of inclination variation on node configuration (quadrature vs syzygy) and observational validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hæc est inclinationis Variatio maxima quatenus locus Lunæ in Orbe suo non consideratur ... Nam inclinatio, si Nodi in Syzygiis versantur, nil mutatur ex vario situ Lunæ. At si Nodi in Quadraturis consistunt, inclinatio major est ubi Luna versatur in Syzygiis, quàm ubi ea versatur in Quadraturis, excessu 2′. 44" ... Atque hæc ita se habere confirmatur ex Observationibus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that maximal inclination variation depends on nodes' configuration: when nodes are in syzygy the inclination is unaffected by lunar longitude, but when nodes are in quadrature, inclination differs between syzygy and quadrature by about 2'44". Use observational data to confirm computed inclination values and the geometric dependence described.
